text: The Feynman Technique is a way of testing real understanding, by explaining ideas out loud. Fun fact — it wasn't actually invented by Feynman himself. Later educators distilled it, from the way he taught.

Its standard is brutal: familiarity is not understanding. You highlight, you re-read, everything looks familiar — and your brain tells you: got it. Only when you can explain it to a complete outsider, do you truly understand.

The method has just four steps. Step one: write the concept down. Step two: explain it to a layperson. Step three: spot the gaps — wherever you get stuck, is exactly what you need to revisit. Step four: simplify with analogies, until anyone can repeat it back. Then loop, until the whole thing flows.
The method is great — but hard to practice. Where do you find a listener, who's always available, knows nothing, and never stops asking questions?
This skill turns the whole method into a system: an AI that plays the listener, plus a set of scripts that record and track everything.
Using it takes one sentence: you explain, it asks. Explain compound interest, and it asks — why would a bank just hand you money? Explain it fully, and you pass. Fall short, and it shows you the gap.
It also enforces discipline: a state machine watches over every step — prepare, probe, wrap up, log. Nothing skipped. Nothing out of order.
Before each session, it does its homework: it researches the new concept, and reviews your history — wherever your old gaps were, that's where it pushes hardest.

Everything is triggered in plain language. Ask, "have I been improving?" — and you get your score trend. Say, "export to Obsidian" — and every conversation becomes study notes. No programming required.
Every pass also becomes a review card: your polished explanation, one analogy, and three transfer quizzes.
The site also hosts real conversations across five fields — finance, AI, math, physics, and psychology. Some pass. Some crash and burn.
Install it with one command: npx skills add. Pick a concept you think you know — and start explaining.
